question.worked_solution:
The first thing we notice is that we can rewrite the terms of the series as powers of $\frac{2}{e}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}1-\frac{2}{e}+\frac{4}{{e}^{2}}-⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}\,{2}^{n}}{{e}^{n}}+⋯ & =1-\frac{2}{e}+\frac{{2}^{2}}{{e}^{2}}+⋯+(-1)^{n}\frac{{2}^{n}}{{e}^{n}}+⋯ \\  & =1-\frac{2}{e}+{(\frac{2}{e})}^{2}+⋯+(-1)^{n}{(\frac{2}{e})}^{n}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we recognize that the series looks similar to the Maclaurin expansion for $f(x)=\frac{1}{1+x}.$

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{1+x} & =1-x+{x}^{2}-{x}^{3}+⋯+(-1)^{n}{x}^{n}+⋯\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting $x=\frac{2}{e}$ into our Maclaurin expansion gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{(1+\frac{2}{e})} & =1-\frac{2}{e}+{(\frac{2}{e})}^{2}-{(\frac{2}{e})}^{3}+⋯+(-1)^{n}{(\frac{2}{e})}^{n}+⋯ \\ \frac{e}{e+2} & =1-\frac{2}{e}+\frac{4}{{e}^{2}}-\frac{8}{{e}^{3}}+⋯+\frac{(-1)^{n}\,{2}^{n}}{{e}^{n}}+⋯.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sum of the series is $\frac{e}{e+2}.$
